As IoT systems shift towards Edge computing and less reliable infrastructure closer to users, the need for robust, adaptable software grows. This demands a testing framework that can efficiently identify and address issues arising from the unpredictable nature of Edge environments. Although various testing tools are available, they often struggle to handle the complex, asynchronous events characteristic of Edge development. In response, we've developed a flexible event-driven testing approach, utilizing the Pytest framework, to accommodate the unique challenges of Edge programming. This method enables the creation of reliable, high-quality Edge software. An example of this approach can be found on the Edge Testing Lab platform. https://edgetestinglab.org/events-driven-testing-for-edge-applications.html?lang=en. This work contributes to the advancement of Edge testing technologies and methodologies. Furthermore, we invite collaboration and the exchange of ideas with the Edge testing community. This includes sharing event-driven testing approaches, best practices, and successful use cases at the Edge Testing Lab community platform. Together, we can develop effective methods for generating reliable software, necessary for the secure operation of Edge systems. The development of autonomous vehicles relies heavily on advanced modeling of road scenes. However, creating realistic 3D scene models is a complex and time-consuming task, which is why it's essential to have efficient methods for generating accurate models. In response to limitations in existing approaches, particularly those based on pairwise models and specialized databases, we've developed a novel scene generation method called SceneGen. SceneGen uses a unique set of points to define the structure of road scenes and uses a corresponding set of semantic attributes to describe the elements within those scenes. By leveraging these descriptions, SceneGen can create detailed 3D scene models through the combination of primitive geometric shapes. To test the effectiveness of SceneGen, we've developed a range of evaluation metrics and compared the method to several baseline approaches, using real-world scene models and real-world testing data to gauge performance. The results show SceneGen to be highly accurate and efficient, outperforming the competition in every category. Furthermore, SceneGen has the added benefit of being able to recover real-world scenes from virtual models, which can be used to enhance training datasets for 3D detection algorithms. The code for SceneGen is available on GitHub at https://github.com/PRIP-UM/SceneGen. The method has also been demonstrated at the IEEE Intelligent Transportation Systems Conference (ITSC) 2022. In the accompanying video, available on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q0xQ5Q1x6Qo, SceneGen is shown generating real-world traffic scenes. High-resolution subsurface modeling through seismic imaging is crucial for understanding complex earth dynamics, informing geothermal and hydrocarbon exploration, and preventing seismic hazards. Despite its limitations, the conventional ray-theory based imaging method, reverse time migration, remains the industry standard due to its computational efficiency. However, this approach falls short in modeling irregular subsurface structures and accurately capturing seismic wave behavior. This study builds upon wave-theory based imaging methods by introducing wavefield-based imaging condition and wavefield reconstruction techniques, specifically the extended source and recursive wavefield reconstruction methods. By utilizing synthetic data, we demonstrate the feasibility of implementing these methods on actual field data, specifically exploring the benefits of extended sources in reconstructing wavefields and accurately capturing seismic wave behavior. This work contributes to the development of more efficient seismic imaging methods that better capture seismic wave behavior and enhance resolution in seismic data. Furthermore, this study provides insights into the design of optimal seismic acquisition and source signatures for wavefield reconstruction and imaging. This research is an important step towards the development of wave-theory based seismic imaging methods that can accurately model complex earth structures and enhance resolution in seismic data. Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with the classical Islamic civilization utilizing the Sun's daily movement to determine prayer times, often relying on sundials for this purpose. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a result of this historical exchange, reflecting a unique blend of astronomical, mathematical, and cultural knowledge. Unfortunately, many historical sundials have disappeared over time, leaving behind only limited documentation and no clear instructions on how they were constructed. This lack of information hinders the ability to accurately determine local standard time, as it is based on the standard time zone established in 1924. To address this issue, researchers have developed an approach that utilizes historical sundials in conjunction with modern technology to promote cultural heritage preservation. This approach involves documenting and reconstructing historical sundials, as exemplified by the demonstration of a 17th-century sundial from the Jakarta Old Town, to make timekeeping accessible to the general public. This fusion of traditional knowledge and modern technology has resulted in an engaging cultural exhibition and an educational initiative, both centered around the theme of time and the Islamic calendar. This interdisciplinary project combines engineering, physics, astronomy, mathematics, computer science, and cultural studies to inspire future research and collaboration among academics and the broader community. This project has culminated in the development of an open-source software for calculating and visualizing local solar time, as well as standard and hijri time, on any date and location. This software has been successfully applied to the reconstruction of the Jakarta National Monument's timekeeper, a historic water clock, and has been made available for download along with the project's documentation and findings. This research has paved the way for exploring other historical timekeeping devices and has demonstrated the potential for cultural heritage preservation through the fusion of traditional knowledge and modern technology. This has resulted in an engaging cultural exhibition and an educational initiative that can be adapted for other communities and historical artifacts. This project has also highlighted the importance of incorporating cultural and historical aspects into the development of technology and software, as well as the value of inter-disciplinary collaboration in addressing complex challenges. This has led to the identification of new research opportunities and potential collaborations with other institutions and organizations. We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when combined with the associated boundary homeomorphisms' actions are considered. This counteracts a previous conjecture linking compactness to topological compactness within certain surface homeomorphism contexts. Additionally, our proof demonstrates that homeomorphisms within a specific category, characterized by the presence of wild arcs, cannot produce compact subgroups. This finding extends to homeomorphisms capable only changing the surface's volume through the creation of wild arcs. This research builds upon previous work by the authors and M. Misiurewicz.

The rapid spread of infectious diseases can be significantly influenced by isolated super-spreader events that result in rapid, extensive transmission. This effect can be modeled by incorporating a single high-transmission node into standard SIR and SIS epidemiological networks. By analyzing various network structures, our findings indicate that the critical node's high transmission rate can substantially increase the speed at which the epidemic spreads, spillover rates remaining equal, and that this increase in spread pace can result in the epidemic's persistence in otherwise disease-resistant networks. Moreover, the critical factor determining this increase in spread pace is found to be the ratio of the high-transmission node's transmission rate to the product of its degree and average neighbor degree, influencing epidemic spread more significantly than node degree alone. This research provides a theoretical framework for exploring the impact of super-spreader events on epidemic spread through analysis and numerical results, supported by a practical application to healthcare worker scheduling. This shows that in epidemics, the critical factor is often not the individual who spreads the disease, but the group that they infect. This implies that targeting high-transmission nodes may not always be the most effective approach in controlling the spread of a disease, and that managing the groups they belong to may be more critical. This concept can be applied across multiple networks, and could have implications for tackling the spread of information and infectious diseases. This leads to the conclusion that controlling the spread of rumors is even more challenging than managing the spread of diseases. Accurate solar vector magnetic field data relies heavily on the inversion of measurements made at different heights above the solar surface. However, these measurements are often influenced by biases, primarily caused by the instrument's limitations and the recovery of the signal as it passes through the solar atmosphere. In this study, we investigate the source of these biases and assess their impact on the inversion process. By applying a statistical correction to the measurements, we demonstrate that it's possible to mitigate their effect and obtain more precise solar magnetic field estimates. This improvement translates to enhanced detection rates for magnetic field fluctuations, as well as more accurate spatial resolution. This finding holds significant implications for the development of inversion techniques, emphasizing the importance of addressing the inherent biases to achieve optimal results. In the context of the specific method used here, an optimization of the inversion code can lead to better performance even without the application of statistical correction. This optimized code is also made available for download alongside this study. In the broader context, this research underscores the need for continuous monitoring of data quality and systematic degradation tests to stay abreast of any changes in the instrument's performance and the solar environment. This is particularly crucial for missions with extended observation periods. In the case of the Helioseismic and Magnetic Instrument on board the Solar Dynamics Observatory, this level of data quality control is essential for the continued monitoring of the evolution of the solar magnetic field. In the long term, this will be a critical consideration for future solar missions with similar instrumentation. This paper investigates the relationship between integers that are y-friable (or y-smooth) and the Dickman function. We begin by defining a probabilistic measure, referred to as density, in conjunction with the $\rho$ function to analyze the proportion of y-friable integers within the range of $[y^n, y^{n+1})$. Our analysis reveals that this proportion converges to $\rho(n/y)$ as $y$ increases without bound. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the underlying density function is intrinsically self-referential, thereby providing an independent verification of T.H. Diamond's conjecture regarding the asymptotic behavior of y-friable integers. We also derive an alternative proof for the result of P. Diamond and A. Erdős concerning the distribution of twin prime pairs. Our proof involves establishing the desired density of pairs at a distance of at least $y$ and then applying the Chinese Remainder Theorem to extend this result to pairs with arbitrary differences. We extend this result to pairs of primes with differences following the sequence $x(\log \log x)^2$, and we also explore the concept of y-friable pairs of integers that are relatively prime. We establish that the probability of two randomly selected integers within this range forming a pair of relatively prime y-friable integers converges to the product of two $\rho$ functions as $y$ increases without bound. We also investigate the broader category of y-friable sets of integers, and we demonstrate that the probability of two randomly selected integers within this range sharing an common factor less than $y$ converges to the square of $\rho$ as $y$ increases without bound. We establish that the probability of two randomly selected integers within this range being congruent modulo a common integer less than $y$ converges to the sum of the squares of $\rho$ as $y$ increases without bound. We also explore the concept of y-friable pairs of integers that are congruent, and we demonstrate that the probability of two randomly selected integers within this range sharing a common factor less than $y$ and being congruent modulo this factor converges to the sum of the product of $\rho$ and its square as $y$ increases without bound. We establish that the probability of two randomly selected integers within this range being congruent modulo a common integer less than $y$ and having a specific quadratic residue property converges to the square of the sum of $\rho$ and its square as $y$ increases without bound.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh kernel (m-ar-K) Fast Independent Component Analysis (FastICA), a novel non-linear dimensionality reduction technique. Based on the kernel trick, this method efficiently transforms data into a higher-dimensional space for independent component analysis (ICA). Unlike other kernel-based ICA methods, FastICA is now capable of non-linear dimensionality reduction after being mapped to a higher-dimensional space. However, using this method in a semi-supervised setting may lead to inconsistent results due to the lack of constraints in the transformation process. To address this issue, we propose augmenting the data with additional synthetic observations, effectively increasing the number of data points available for analysis while aligning them with prior knowledge. This approach is then implemented in a kernel-based context, allowing the application of m-ar-K FastICA in a semi-supervised settings. Furthermore, we explore the parameters of this method, including the choice of kernel type and hyperparameters. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through a range of synthetic datasets and real-world benchmark datasets. Notably, m-ar-K FastICA achieves superior results in the MNIST dataset, outperforming other dimensionality reduction techniques in subsequent classification tasks. The source code for this research is available online. The findings indicate that the choice of kernel type has a more significant impact on classification performance than the number of components retained. This research provides a novel method for combining ICA and semi-supervised learning, extending the capabilities of ICA in a semi-supervised context while facilitating the integration of prior knowledge into the analysis. Furthermore, we explore the application of this approach to the analysis of brain imaging data. By comparing the performance of different dimensionality reduction techniques, we identify areas for improvement and potential avenues for methodological development. This work offers an overview of requirements engineering in the gaming sector.
This industry's requirements are unique, with massive financial stakes and the creation of interactive, long-lasting products that cater to diverse consumer needs.
To succeed, developers must consider multiple aspects, including artistic vision, technical capabilities, and commercial goals.
This paper will discuss various approaches to managing these complexities, with a focus on general strategies rather than specific case studies.
It examines the use of formal methods, collaborative tools, and customer feedback to shape requirements, as well as the role of vision documents, prototypes, and storyboarding in communicating requirements to the development team.
It also explores how risk management, quality assurance, and Agile methods influence the requirements engineering process.
This work aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of how requirements are managed in the gaming industry, with potential applications in other fields that involve complex, high-stakes development projects. This knowledge can be used to inform the development of more effective requirements engineering guidelines tailored to the gaming sector. This is particularly relevant given the growing presence of digital games in fields like education, healthcare, and transportation, which highlights the need for a deeper understanding of how requirements are managed in this industry. This understanding can, in turn, contribute to producing higher-quality software that better meets the needs of its players. To analyze the impact of external magnetic field on doped nematic superconductor $\mathrm{Cu}_2(\mathrm{Te}_2_\mathrm{Se}_2)$, we employ the itinerant triplon model and consider long-range nematic dipole dipole interactions. In the presence of strong nematic order and low temperature, we find that the cost of triplon's spin freedom is minimized when its spin is directly aligned with the external magnetic field, resulting in a paramagnetic response similar to that of Pauli. Notably, this effect is observable only in nematic superconductors and could be measured through magnetization near a nematic-superconducting interface. Additionally, we observe that the nematic-superconducting state exhibits contrasting behaviors between its interior and the region near the interface. This distinction arises due to differing orbital motions' symmetries in these areas, causing triplons' interactions to exhibit both nematic and chiral properties near the interface, while only displaying nematic characteristics inside. This unique property may influence the behavior of quasiparticles in these regions. Furthermore, we discover that the nematic-superconducting state's interior can also exhibit a chiral ground state, achieved through a drive that suppresses nematic order while maintaining triplon's superconducting state. This transformation, however, demands precise control over external influences to prevent the nematic order from reinstating. This finding opens a pathway to experimentally identify a chiral superconducting state through the detection of Pauli paramagnetic response near a nematic-superconducting interface. This could also shed light on the long-standing debate about whether nematic superconductors can exhibit chiral properties. causal relationships. A corresponding task, reverse retrieval, is defined to
investigate whether current models can recognize patterns and relationships implied
by specific instances. Our research reveals that these models excel at recalling
past events given their characteristics but struggle to anticipate future events and
their consequences based on given premises. Our findings indicate a significant
disparity between the ability to recall factual information and the ability to use
that information to make predictions, highlighting a critical gap in the current
state of natural language processing. Our dataset and tasks are designed to foster

innovative approaches to the reverse retrieval task. We anticipate that further
exploration of the ATOMIC atlas will yield valuable insights into the nature of

Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational complexity hinders traditional methods for rapid decision-making. Recently, portfoliodynamics was proposed, offering a solution to the mean-variance portfolio optimization problem and enabling fast, approximate answers using quantum computing. This approach involves two challenging quantum computations: the simulation of asset time-series dynamics and the estimation of asset co-variances. While co-variance estimation can be achieved through an efficient quantum algorithm, simulating asset time-series dynamics is not currently feasible with sufficient accuracy on quantum computers. In this work, we introduce a hybrid approach that leverages both quantum and classical computing to overcome this hurdle. By combining the Heisenberg-Lanczos method with machine learning and classical portfolio optimization techniques, we develop a solution that accelerates quantum computing convergence while delivering precise results, showcasing its advantages over the classical approach. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach for a set of real-world assets and demonstrate its scalability to a range of portfolio sizes. Notably, this work marks the first application of the Heisenberg-Lanczos method in quantum computing, and we anticipate that our findings will pave the way for the successful deployment of quantum computing in finance. Furthermore, this research will be executed on the IBM Quantum System, providing a blueprint for the acceleration of convergent quantum algorithms on near-term quantum hardware. This work has been accepted for presentation at the 2023 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and an asymptotic distribution for the empirical measure of the first $k_n$ parking locations. This study involves a non-reversible Markov chain, specifically one generated by a random permutation of size $n$, and the analysis employs phase transitions in recursive structures. This analysis may be applicable to other problems involving recursive structures exhibiting non-trivial phase transitions. Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our method can generate videos from significantly wider angles, such as 90 degrees, between the training and prediction views. The core of the approach is based on two separate representations: a view-agnostic model and a view-dependent model. The view-agnostic model produces a general, training-view-specific representation, while the view-dependent model generates view-specific details. These representations are combined through a dual representation decoder, allowing the model to account for both general and unique features across views. Notably, the view-dependent model is trained using a novel multi-view training mask, allowing it to focus on unique features present only in the target view. Experimental results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on novel view video prediction tasks, surpassing existing approaches by a significant margin. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems and is thought to induce topological properties. Our study on Co/Bi multilayers reveals that increased scattering at the interface can enhance this effect, potentially overcoming the limitations of intrinsic Spin-Orbit Coupling in a specific material. By comparing different materials, we found that choosing a suitable proximate material could result in a substantial increase in Spin-Orbit Coupling, even without considering the material's intrinsic properties. This finding provides a new approach to designing materials with enhanced Spin-Orbit Coupling and may facilitate the creation of topological materials. However, the optimal interface should have a low scattering rate to minimize carrier localization and restore the material's original properties. This research was conducted using X-ray diffraction, magnetometry, and electrical transport measurements on Co/Bi multilayers. The results indicate that the spin-orbit proximity effect can lead to an increase in Spin-Orbit Coupling, and this enhancement may be a universal phenomenon applicable to other materials. Sequential neural network models like LSTMs are designed to process linearly ordered sequences, yet they can effectively analyze complex structures within these sequences. This study explores the connection between the linguistic concept of subject-verb agreement and sequential models' ability to capture this relationship. It focuses on the verb agreement patterns in the Basque language, which are heavily influenced by the grammatical gender of the subject. Although the gender information appears only once in the subject noun phrase, the agreement is reflected fully in the past participle. In this context, the study discovers that while LSTMs are generally capable of modeling this agreement, their performance is often subpar when compared to a specialized model that incorporates the gender information present in the subject noun phrase. This finding suggests that LSTMs are able to recognize the agreement but struggle to retain the relevant information across the sequence. This limitation is attributed to the fact that neural network models rely on the activation of specific neurons to capture the agreement, which can be difficult to maintain over long sequences. This study provides a theoretical framework that explains how LSTMs can capture the agreement by retaining the agreement information in the hidden state at each sequence position. This framework is then applied to design a novel agreement-based objective function that is used to train LSTMs to capture the agreement. This new objective function is shown to significantly outperform the standard cross-entropy objective function on the task of predicting the past participle given the subject noun phrase. This improvement is observed across multiple LSTMs of varying sizes, indicating that the proposed objective function is a robust solution to enhancing the agreement-capturing abilities of sequential neural network models. This study also explores the generalization of this agreement-based objective function to other sequence classification tasks. It discovers that the ability to capture the agreement is a common problem in these tasks, which are characterized by the presence of internal cues within the sequence that influence the target label. This is demonstrated through the application of this proposed objective function to multiple such tasks, including the prediction of the past participle in the presence of negation, the prediction of the past participle given the subject and negation, and the prediction of the adjective form given the subject and negation. This study shows that the proposed objective function leads to a significant improvement over the standard cross-entropy objective function on these tasks. We calculate the one-loop central-emission vertex for two gluons in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory, extending the existing helicity amplitude calculations in this context. This emission vertex is a key component in determining the helicity amplitudes for multiple gluon scatterings. We derived the central-emission vertex in question using the amplitude fixation method, first introduced by Berghahn, Jaskolla, and van daalen. We found this vertex to contribute significantly to the helicity amplitudes, particularly noticeable in the low-energy range. Notably, this calculation reveals that the one-loop central-emission vertex alone is sufficient to reproduce the known helicity amplitudes in this energy range, contradicting earlier assumptions that this vertex's contribution would be negligible. We also observed that the real part of this vertex, obtained through the amplitude fixation method, closely matches the corresponding part derived from the on-shell recursion relation, with the exception of certain color channels. We found that the discrepancy arises from an additional contribution stemming from the on-shell recursion relation itself, specifically from the interaction between the recursion relation's "glue" function and the two-gluon central-emission vertex. Notably, this additional component can be accounted for by the recursion relation alone, without the need for additional input. We have made the results of this calculation available in the form of tables and figures within this document. These results provide valuable insights into the non-linear nature of the strong interaction, as they demonstrate that the interaction between individual gluons gives rise to the observed energy dependencies in the helicity amplitudes. The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system, which developed as a result of plate movement away from the Atlantic-Mediterranean hotspots, specifically the Rio Grande do Norte hotspot, during the Cretaceous period. This paper focuses on the kinematics of the South Atlantic rift by analyzing the geometry of the basin's bordering passive margins. It identifies key features such as the curved shape of the margin, the presence of offset rifts, and the variation in rift basin width. It then uses these geometric observations to develop a comprehensive model describing the kinematics of the rift. This model consists of multiple, interconnected shear zones that controlled the extensional deformation during the rifting period. It also includes a system of faults that influenced the migration of the rift valleys and the rotation of shear zones. This model was tested using numerical simulations that replicated the geometric patterns of the rift valleys. It was found that the timing of the rifting phase, the orientation of the beta factor, and the rate of extensional deformation played significant roles in shaping the geometry of the South Atlantic rift. This research provides valuable insights for the improved modeling of hydrocarbon reservoirs and sedimentary basins that are currently forming in areas of extensional tectonic activity. This is because the model highlights the importance of considering the effects of irregular rift migration and the impact it has on the surrounding sedimentary deposits. This is particularly relevant for the South Atlantic margin, where the discovery of significant oil and gas reserves in deepwater provinces has created a need for more advanced modeling techniques. This research can also be applied to other intraplate rift systems, such as the East African rift system, by identifying the key factors that contribute to irregular rift migration and the resulting geometric patterns. This is because understanding the kinematics of these systems is crucial for the accurate modeling of their geometry and the hydrocarbon reservoirs that they contain. A detailed investigation into the origins of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem was conducted. This investigation involved examining the most fundamental characteristics of NG bosons, including their irreducibility, absence in coupled theories, and singular propagation characteristics. The analysis demonstrated that coupled NG modes no longer appear as single-component fields. Furthermore, the process of combining multiple fields to describe a single physical mode eliminates the singular propagation characteristics associated with that mode's individual component. The concept of a NG mode being non-dynamical is shown to arise inherently from the properties of a given symmetry-breaking pattern rather than resulting from the mode's individual dynamical characteristics. Consequently, the existence of a NG mode within a given theory is sufficient to guarantee the presence of a NG boson, rendering the explicit demonstration of a NG mode's non-dynamical nature unnecessary. The applicability of the anomalous NG theorem was further confirmed by applying the theorem's principles to the U(1) symmetry-breaking case and deriving the existence of a NG boson within the electroweak theory at its symmetry restoration point without relying on non-renormalizable effective potential interactions. The impossibility of coupling a single NG mode was demonstrated by showing that attempting to couple such a mode would instead result in the decomposition of the mode into multiple component fields, each of which would then become a NG mode. The general validity of the anomalous NG theorem was proven by demonstrating that the NG modes of a given symmetry-breaking pattern remain intact and irreducible in the presence of perturbations, provided that these perturbations do not give rise to the formation of instabilities in the vacuum state. The impossibility of coupling an NG mode was further confirmed by analyzing the SU(2) symmetry-breaking case and demonstrating that the NG modes derived from this symmetry-breaking pattern become massive in the process of symmetry breaking rather than remaining massless. The distinction between the types of symmetry breaking was highlighted, with spontaneous symmetry breaking being shown to be the only type that can result in the generation of NG modes. The application of the anomalous NG theorem to the weak vector bosons was demonstrated by showing that these modes become massive in the process of symmetry breaking and that their masses are generated through the decomposition of the SU(2) symmetry group rather than resulting from the presence of a zero-momentum mode. The derivation of the Lagrangian for the electroweak theory was provided, with the demonstration that the Lagrangian for the weak vector bosons can be expressed in terms of the SU(2) symmetry

Recent studies have shown that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and flexible models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are severely limited when sourced from human-generated datasets. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework called DISCO that leverages pre-trained LLMs to generate high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale. We achieve this by distilling the expertise of LLMs to anticipate phrasal counterfactuals in a supervised manner. We experimentally demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained to produce such counterffectuals can effectively classify classification tasks with a high degree of accuracy, even when tested against datasets with significant label noise. Moreover, our results indicate that these expert models exhibit a level of robustness against dataset shifts and adversarial attacks. Furthermore, we uncover that the performance of our model is significantly enhanced when it is trained to produce counterfactual data in the form of a continuous representation, a technique we term as PCF. We make the code and data for PCF available at https://github.com/PranavSingh95/PCF. Although PCF is presented within the context of DISCO, it holds the potential to be a standalone method for enhancing the performance of LLMs in various tasks. Research into remote epitaxy holds significant promise, enabling the growth of
lateral films through chemical vapor deposition by exposing a substrate to
irradiated gas. Achieving this method requires precise control over the balance
between three competing growth modes: van der Waals, pinhole, and remote
epitaxy. However, the exact mechanisms underlying these modes remain poorly
understood, particularly in relation to the properties of the substrate and
interface. This study focuses on the growth of the Heusler compound GdFeTe$_3$,
examining how the balance of these modes is affected by the presence of a
graphene monolayer on the substrate. By comparing remote and near-infrared
irradiation, the results reveal that the presence of graphene significantly
reduces the number of pinholes, thereby promoting remote epitaxy. Notably,
irradiation at a wavelength of 450 nm appears to create reactive oxygen species
that hinder the growth, leading to an increase in pinholes and van der Waals
islands. Conversely, near-infrared irradiation generates less reactive oxygen, resulting in improved remote epitaxy. Furthermore, the findings suggest that remote epitaxy can be optimized by selecting materials with high thermal and chemical stability, capable of resisting the reactive oxygen species generated during irradiation. The outcomes of this study provide valuable insights into the mechanisms governing remote epitaxy and highlight the potential of this method for growing a wide range of materials. The results indicate that remote epitaxy can be achieved not only with substrates exposed to irradiated gas but also with heated films exposed to ambient gas, a process that researchers propose calling "remote epitaxy under ambient conditions." This new method holds promise for the controlled growth of films through chemical vapor deposition. The outcomes of this study demonstrate the feasibility of remote epitaxy under ambient conditions for the Heusler compound GdFeTe$_3$, resulting in high-quality films with low magnetic residual impurities. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse mapping for states, by showing that a given state can lead to isomorphic representation spaces. This is equivalent to stating that there is an adjunction at play, specifically a weak adjunction with involvement of 2-categorial natural transformations, which captures the essence of this relationship. Furthermore, this adjunction-based description provides a framework that allows us to incorporate additional physical characteristics, such as symmetries. This is achieved through the use of functor categories for symmetries, which act on both the algebra and its representation space. This approach ensures that physical information, including symmetries, is preserved throughout the mapping between states, observables, and Hilbert spaces. This concept has been specifically exemplified using the category of symmetric monoidal category, but the principles can be applied across a broader range of categories. This work offers a formal description of the relationship between physical states, observables, and Hilbert spaces using category theory, which provides an intuitive understanding of the connection between abstract physical theories and their associated mathematical structures. This understanding can further contribute to the development of abstract mathematical descriptions of physical theories. This research has been motivated by the principles of structural localisation, an approach to formulating the relationship between physical theories and their mathematical representations. This involves analyzing the connection between the abstract, conceptual structure of physical theories and the concrete, specific mathematical representations that they utilize. This research can also be seen as an extension of the ideas presented in the companion paper, where the focus was on describing the mapping between physical states and Hilbert spaces using 2-categorial functors. This study examines the two-dimensional return distribution of a stock portfolio, which is based on the returns of its individual components. By utilizing a non-parametric method to estimate the probability density function, we can analyze the portfolio's distribution and key statistical measures. We demonstrate that certain characteristics of the stock market, such as the number of listed companies, do not significantly impact the shape of the portfolio's distribution. Conversely, we find that certain industry-based portfolios exhibit return distributions that resemble the gamma distribution, particularly when they consist of a small number of highly correlated stocks. We also investigate the skewness of corporate bond portfolios and find that their returns can be optimized through the selection of underlying securities. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this research to topics like portfolio performance evaluation and asset pricing theory. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data is fragmented and isolated on personal devices, secondly, data privacy concerns prevent users from freely sharing their personal health data, and thirdly, models trained on user data data often fail to generalize well to other users. To address these issues, we propose a novel federated transfer learning framework called FedHealth, capable of conducting batched federated learning, adapting to new classes, and achieving high performance without compromising data security. FedHealth successfully integrates multiple techniques, including batched federated learning, wrapper-based transfer learning, and reinforcement learning to optimize performance. Experimental results show FedHealth outperforms traditional transfer learning methods by a significant margin, achieving 92.4% accuracy on activity recognition, 91.6% on sleep pattern recognition, and 96.5% on sports video recognition classification. This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. Consequently, it is essential to strike a balance between model complexity and the availability of relevant data when modeling epidemics. Ultimately, this study advocates for a holistic approach to modeling epidemics, combining expertise from mathematics, computer science, and life sciences to derive actionable insights that inform critical policy decisions. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise determination of the underlying symmetry of the energy spectrum. Notably, the study of topological states has expanded beyond electronic systems to encompass photonic, mechanical, and optical systems, revealing analogous concepts and associated quantities that topologically distinguish these systems's spectra. This review focuses on another vital aspect of topological physics – nodal lines, discrete circles or shapes where the energy gap of the underlying system practically disappears. We discuss the distinctive characteristics of nodal lines, their interconnection with the Weyl points, and the various methods to classify them. Furthermore, this review covers various recent realizations of nodal lines in photonic, phononic, mechanical, and optical systems, and it provides a comprehensive overview of the theoretical concepts associated with these phenomena. It is essential to note that the review's scope is limited to nodal lines associated with the non-zero angular momentum, and it does not cover the vast body of literature on zero-angular momentum nodal lines, which are protected by spatial symmetry rather than the angular momentum one. We believe that this review will be beneficial for both experimental and theoretical researchers working on topological systems. It is our hope that it will help to bridge the gap between theoretical concepts and the photonic systems used to realize them, ultimately facilitating a deeper understanding of the former through the latter. We also anticipate that this review will contribute to an increased interest in the topological physics of nodal lines, which are lines rather than points, and that it will provide a solid foundation for future breakthroughs in this exciting field of research. Differentiable rendering has gained significant traction in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods. However, the field still lacks a comprehensive understanding of the relationships between rendering models, photometric losses, and reconstruction methods. In this work, we introduce an efficient and differentiable shadow computation method that leverages screen-space ray marching. By building on screen-space depth values and incorporating view-direction information, we can achieve precise reconstructions of object shapes, even in areas with complex shadows. A theoretical analysis of the differentiability of this algorithm reveals its individual components' differentiability, allowing for the computation of gradients with respect to object shapes, light sources, and other rendering inputs. We demonstrate the advantages of using this shadow computation method in the context of two image-based inverse problems: deblurring and denoising. Through a thorough evaluation of the effects of light sources and object shapes' smoothness, we provide valuable insights into the design of future models and reconstructions. This paper also presents a practical application for a deinterlacing model pre-trained on a large dataset, demonstrating its potential for real-world use. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations effectively model this phenomenon, their numerical solution can be computationally expensive. In this research, a deep learning approach is explored to leverage the underlying physics encoded in the shallow water equations, with the aim of developing a fast and accurate method to solve these equations. We propose a deep learning-based fast numerical solution method that utilizes the equations' characteristics and combines the advantages of the finite difference method and the advection diffusion equation. This novel algorithm leverages the boundary conditions and river flow velocity data to generate predictions. Our experiments demonstrate that this deep learning-based algorithm can produce accurate predictions, outperforming traditional machine learning methods and matching the performance of the finite difference method. Notably, this algorithm can make predictions significantly faster than the traditional method. This research lays the groundwork for further exploration of the integration of physics-informed neural networks and traditional numerical methods, potentially leading to even more efficient and accurate predictive models. Our model has the potential to be employed in real-world settings, such as in the monitoring of river flows, with the support of high-performance computing. This allows the survey to explore the implications of the interdependence of data on the learning of neural networks and the role of causal knowledge within this context. This paper examines the age of information (AoI) in a discrete-time status updating system that employs the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-dimensional state vector which simultaneously monitors AoI and packet age enables derivation of the stationary AoI distribution via analysis of a critical probability. This probability, indicative of the AoI performance, is derived in the context of the Bernoulli/G/1/1 queue, revealing that the AoI distribution converges to a limiting mixture probability distribution as time progresses. We investigate this convergence in detail, including characterizing the limiting distribution, convergence rates for specific service processes, and conditions under which convergence is guaranteed. Moreover, we develop an efficient algorithm to compute the stationary AoI distribution, leveraging discrete-time queueing properties to streamline calculations compared to existing methods. Ultimately, evaluating AoI performance in discrete-time status updating systems with queues highlights the significance of considering the interplay between AoI, packet age, and service processes. This understanding enables the development of effective strategies to minimize AoI, thereby enhancing the performance of these systems. We also illustrate the applicability of our findings through a real-world use case, demonstrating the potential of the proposed algorithm to provide practical solutions in such scenarios. This work delves into various quantum algebras that arise from a special type of set-theoretic solution to the Yang-Baxter equation and their underlying degree properties. We establish links between these quantum algebras and quasi-bialgebras, and explore how they can be defined using the quantum shuffle product. Specifically, we show that combining the quantum shuffle product with certain degree-preserving twists on the Basserle algebra leads to degree-2 quasi-bialgebras. This connection enables us to derive new set-theoretic solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation from its predecessors, and in doing so, we obtain corresponding quantum algebras and quasi-bialgebras. Lastly, we identify opportunities for further research in this field.

The speed at which astronomical research advances accelerates with the collaboration of multiple telescopes, a phenomenon known as Synoptic Sky Surveying. This cross-correlation of data is further enhanced when combining wide-field surveys. Building on the success of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, SDSS-V will employ a network of large-area telescopes in motion, capable of capturing red fluxes emanating from the Milky Way. This innovative system consists of six telescopes working in unison, with four of them being astrobots that coordinate their observations with the remaining two fixed-normals. The safe coordination of these astrobots is a complex problem, with multiple solutions existing across various disciplines. Notably, the airline industry employs resolutions to its own variant of this problem, known as the conflict resolution problem, when managing conflicts between aircraft. This paper compares the performance of different solutions by testing them on real-world scenarios, with the aim of informing the development of software for managing the astrobots' schedules. Four solutions were evaluated: the model predictive control method, with variants using linear and nonlinear functions; a dynamic matrix control approach; and a simple rule-based system. The results showed that the model predictive control method with nonlinear functions yielded the fewest number of corrections, a key indicator of a system's stability. This approach also produced schedules that minimized the time difference between the fixed and moving telescopes, further indicating a more stable system. This method's advantage in terms of correction frequency was significant, with the rule-based system requiring nearly three times as many corrections. This finding suggests that implementing a more complex solution like the model predictive control method with nonlinear functions could lead to a more stable system, with potential benefits extending to future surveys like the Dark Energy Sky Survey. This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas affected by Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data from a specific region of the marmoset monkey brain. Parkinson's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder primarily caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons within the substantia nigra, a key component of the basal ganglia. Abnormal activities within the basal ganglia circuit lead to movement-related disorders characteristic of the disease. To better comprehend Parkinson's dynamics and develop effective treatments, computational models incorporating brain connectivity and neural systems have proven valuable. By integrating an conductance-based Hodgkin-Huxley type spiking neural network with phase-laminar local field potential models, we successfully recreated the electrophysiological properties of the substantia nigra pars compacta and striatum. Furthermore, we incorporated a comprehensive basal ganglia circuit connectivity model derived from magnetic resonance imaging and diffusion tensor imaging data of the marmoset monkey brain. By analyzing the computational model's results in normal and Parkinsonian conditions, our findings indicate that the model can replicate the abnormally synchronized activity observed in Parkinson's disease and the contrasting asynchronous activity in the control group. Additionally, we discovered that the model's Parkinsonian state could be restored to a normal condition through the application of deep brain stimulation at specific frequencies. This research provides valuable insights into the computational mechanisms underlying Parkinson's disease and may contribute to the development of more effective treatment strategies. Additionally, the model's focus on the marmoset monkey brain may facilitate a more direct translation of computational findings to clinical applications. The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how non-linear small-x saturation impacts shift the Borel plane's initial IR pole from $2/\beta_2$ to $1/\beta_2$, thereby altering the estimated uncertainty to approximately $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^2$ instead of $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^4$. This change occurs at sufficiently low values of x, where the dipole's variance is connected to the gluon's impact factor, specifically for the case of a colorless quark probe. Furthermore, the shift in IR pole is associated with the dipole's ability to probe large gluon 'targets', where the transition from the dilute to the dense regime significantly amplifies the dominant $2/\beta_2$ IR renormalon. The estimated $x$-dependence of the initial IR renormalon is derived from an approximate, but explicit calculation of the dipole's variance in the saturation regime, and the resulting $x$-dependence can be used to gauge the influence of IR renormalons on the JIMMWY impact factor at small-x. The analysis reveals that the uncertainty associated with IR renormalons is dominated by the $2/\beta_2$ pole and increases with decreasing x, but remains below expected logarithmic accuracy and is generally in line with expectations based on the BFKL backbone of the JIMMWY impact factor. The study also highlights the significance of non-linear small-x effects, which enhance the impact of the $2/\beta_2$ IR renormalon to the point where it becomes the dominant uncertainty for sufficiently low values of x. The findings suggest that the $2/\beta_2$ IR renormalon's influence on the JIMMWY impact factor at small-x is primarily driven by the onset of non-linear small-x saturation, which shifts the probe from interacting with a set of independent gluons to interacting with a dense, interacting gluon 'target'. The influence of this transition on the estimated uncertainty is so significant that even if the $1/\beta_2$ IR pole dominates the time it spends within the Borel plane, the resulting uncertainty will still be comparable to that of the $2/\beta_2$ pole once the probe's non-linear small-x effects are fully accounted for. The study's conclusions are robust and applicable to a range of phenomenological applications at small-x, including deep virtual Compton scattering

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by successfully training models for classification, segmentation, and GAN generation using a black-box model as the teacher, even without access to the training data. Notably, the results show that the network can learn to recognize patterns and generalize to new data with just a few examples. This problem has been proven to be NP-complete for all graphs. We investigate the classic problem of efficient imitation learning using an imperfect training set, drawing from a well-studied framework established by Ross et al. We focus on the scenario where the training examples significantly deviate from optimal behavior. We establish a fundamental bound indicating that the quality of imitation learning is limited by an interplay between the data's reliability and the optimality target. Notably, this bound reveals that no algorithm can achieve optimal performance unless the training data and target policy are identical. We further develop a new algorithm, TRAIL, that provides a groundbreaking guarantee. Under the assumption that the training examples and target policy follow a linear dynamics structure, TRAIL achieves the near-optimal performance by precisely narrowing the gap to the optimal bound. We validate our theoretical findings with comprehensive imitation learning experiments on various complex tasks. The results consistently show that TRAIL surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, offering a substantial improvement in particular on difficult tasks requiring a large number of expert demonstrations. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimental results show that CoIL not only outperforms single-agent reinforcement learning but also expert demonstration-based imitation learning methods, even without access to expert knowledge. Moreover, we analyze the advantages of using peer agents over natural exploration alone, demonstrating a substantial improvement in learning efficiency, especially in complex tasks and when the reward signal is weak. driving force. The system is also affected by its own losses. We develop a

The LAMOST Time-Domain Survey officially began observations in December 2015, and has been collecting data ever since on targets across four $K$2 plates.  Initial results reveal that nearly 3000 eclipsing binary stars exhibit orbital periods ranging from 0.47 days to 636.26 days, with a notable peak at 2.62 days.  Furthermore, 1347 such binary stars demonstrated period changes, while 1245 showed little to no change.  In terms of long-period variables, 1415 targets with pulsation periods ranging from 0.43 days to 1551 days were identified.  In addition, 11 candidate pulsating subdwarf $B$ and 6 candidate white dwarf stars were discovered through their photometric variations.  In total, 2,620,000 light curves were obtained over 207 nights, with an average exposure time of 480 seconds per frame. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly regarding how they maintain consistency. In this paper, we provide a clear and concise description of the transactional protocols used in MongoDB's three deployment types, verifying that they do, in fact, guarantee the consistency specified by MongoDB's documentation. This validation is essential for ensuring that MongoDB's transactions adhere to the PSR standard, which is a set of guidelines for building atomic, cross-document applications in NoSQL databases. By reviewing the verification process, we also outline the challenges encountered when validating the transactional protocols used in MongoDB's distributed deployments. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the development of applications that utilize MongoDB's transactions. This verification process can serve as a model for evaluating the consistency of other database transactions. In the context of MongoDB, this work can contribute to improving the accuracy of the documentation related to its transactional protocols. Additionally, it can facilitate the development of more effective tools for debugging and verifying applications that utilize MongoDB's transactions. This verification process can also be used to inform the design of future database standards and best practices. In the conclusion, we outline the potential for extending this validation process to other database standards and protocols. To understand the magnetic and structural behavior of Aurivillius Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ under high pressure, we employed nuclear forward scattering in conjunction with synchrotron X-ray diffraction.  At ambient pressure, this material exhibits ferrimagnetic properties due to the interaction between high-spin Fe$^{3+$.  Upon increasing pressure to 24.6 GPa, we observed a structural phase transition from tetragonal to orthorhombic, accompanied by a significant reduction in the magnetic moment, despite the expected increase in high-spin state energy under pressure.  Conversely, a high pressure of 34.5 GPa resulted in the re-emergence of the initial magnetic moment, coupled with the structural phase transitioning back to the tetragonal symmetry.  We propose that the intermediate orthorhombic phase may be stabilized by the distortion caused by the TiO$_8$ antiprisms, which could have implications for the design of materials with mixed cations under pressure.  This study also highlights the utility of combining nuclear forward scattering and synchrotron X-ray diffraction to gain a comprehensive understanding of the structural and magnetic behavior of materials under high pressure. In epitaxial InAs/Al structures, our experimental findings reveal the stochastic behavior of planar Josephson junctions and SQUIDs as temperature varies, exhibiting a crossover between macroscopic quantum tunneling and phase diffusion. The threshold temperature for this phase transition, T*, can be manipulated through material properties by adjusting the thickness of the planar weak link. A theoretical model incorporating a quasi-one-dimensional superconducting channel connects T* to a critical width, λc, and reveals that the switching current distribution is influenced by both T* and temperature-independent factors. The results of our experiments and modeling suggest that planar Josephson junctions and SQUIDs can serve as precise probes for dynamical phase transitions in one dimension. Furthermore, the simplicity of these devices makes them suitable for integrating switching current measurements with other quantum operations in planar architectures. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, the square root of the expected squared delta, and the time to maturity. Consequently, this formulation enables the derivation of closed-form expressions for various hedging cost metrics, including Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall. Notably, this approach enables the integration of option margin calculations with other risk assessments, such as those for stocks and bonds, allowing for a holistic aggregation of hedging costs within a portfolio. Furthermore, this approach is adaptable to accommodate multiple delta-hedging frequencies, resulting in a comprehensive and practical framework for option margin calculation. The fraction of light from these features is much higher, at 11.5%, indicating they are prominent. We calculated the merger rate of massive early-type galaxies based on tidal features and found it to be 0.023 times the rate at which such galaxies form per Gyr, in a cubic megaparsec. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers a framework for evaluating policy changes, such as expanding access to opportunities. The model assumes that each generation makes independent decisions. The allocation mechanism we suggest is a dynamic version of the classic Gale-Shapley algorithm, commonly used to find optimal matches in a static model. The proposed method ensures that the most beneficial opportunities are matched with the most beneficial recipients in each period. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections, the network seamlessly integrates the insights from both domains, producing a comprehensive feature set that enhances classification performance. Experimentation reveals the efficacy of this method, with the achievement of state-of-the-art accuracy on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Data Sets. Notably, our method demonstrates superior performance when compared to current state-of-the-art deepfake detection models in terms of robustness and adaptability. The implementation of the frequency spectrum processing component allows the network to operate efficiently, with minimal computational overhead. The integration of the frequency branch also facilitates the detection of deepfake audio with only spatial domain processing. The open-source code and model for the proposed MD-CSDNetwork are available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zheng-xy/md-csdnet. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs. Notably, our research provides a framework for exploring the broader implications of degree-degree correlations in LDPC codes. In addition, we demonstrate that degree-degree correlated LDPC codes can be efficiently decoded using a simple iterative soft-input soft-output (SISO) decoder, with a complexity comparable to that of conventional LDPC decoders. To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile devices and the rising demand for mobile data, next-generation cellular networks must shift from traditional, human-centric approaches to resource management. This requires an automatic system that adapts to changing conditions and optimizes performance across multiple metrics. This paper introduces a new resource allocation strategy for uplink OFDMA cellular networks, where a central controller rapidly makes decisions to minimize delay, while also optimizing throughput and reducing waste. This is achieved by dividing the network into areas based on the strength of the signal, and allocating resources within these regions to maximize data transfer. This strategy is compared and contrasted with a method that uses fixed zones, and both theoretically, and through simulation and field testing, we show the benefits of dynamic management. This leads to improved performance in areas with frequent mobile device connectivity, such as airports and shopping centers. This work also informs the design of future self-organizing cellular networks, and suggests potential applications for other networks facing similar challenges. This research is now available as an open-source project, available for use and further development. In the context of a graph, learning occurs when multiple machines, connected in a network, collaborate to improve their models based on shared and private data. We present an efficient new method, DR-DSGD, for training neural networks in a decentralized manner on graphs. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on assumptions of having similar data distributions, DR-DSGD protects models from overfitting to specific samples. Instead of optimizing model parameters directly, DR-DSGD minimizes the discrepancy in predicted outputs across neighboring nodes, thus preventing models from fitting too closely to local data. Through predicted output transfer, models learn to capture more general features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DR-DSGD through experiments showing it achieves comparable performance to non-robust methods on datasets with homogeneous data, while significantly outperforming them on datasets with heterogeneous data, in both classification and decentralized model training scenarios. Notably, DR-DSGD's performance in the latter case matches that of robust methods while being more efficient and practical. We also examine the influence of different hyperparameters and provide a robust implementation of DR-DSGD. Furthermore, we explore the application of DR-DSGD to learning in non-regular graph topologies by developing a new measure of diversity in output predictions. This output prediction diversity measure allows DR-DSGD to learn in topologies that are cyclic or fully connected. We show the generalization of DR-DSGD to learning in a federation of machines by introducing a new sampling method, and demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through additional experiments. This historical analysis examines the development of computer simulations in the study of hard disks from the early days of molecular dynamics simulations through to recent advances. Noting the progress made over the past seven decades, the paper emphasizes the need for a more in-depth exploration of the interplay between computer simulations and theoretical models. A specific case study of hard disks is particularly productive in this regard, given the relative ease with which their behavior can be simulated and the simplicity of the pair-correlation theory that describes their static properties. In examining the evolution of simulations, from the initial methods of 1940s-style Monte Carlo simulations via the MD simulations of the 1950s to contemporary algorithms, the paper highlights both the scientific and technical factors that influenced the choice of simulation methods over time. A discussion of various attempts to measure the pair-correlation function using simulations is also included, along with an analysis of the role of computer power in driving the growth from small-scale simulations in the 1950s to today's massive simulations. Finally, the paper considers the current challenges facing simulations of hard disks at high densities, including the limitations imposed by the availability of computer resources and the difficulties of achieving equilibrium configurations through gaseous, solid, and liquid phase simulations simultaneously. Furthermore, the paper raises the question of whether it is possible to achieve a high degree of accuracy in the comparison of simulations with theoretical predictions, particularly in regions of phase space that are difficult to access. The paper also includes a discussion of the implications of its findings for the broader field of soft-sphere simulations. The historical analysis presented in the paper is set within the context of the author's own research on hard disks spanning over five decades. The author, who is currently an emeritus professor, reflects on the evolution of computer simulations and the lessons that can be applied to the training of the next generation of researchers. The paper is an expansion of the author's previous report, which was delivered at the XVIII Argentine School of Computational Physics held in 2018. In this study, a significant near-ultraviolet flare of the active star AD Leo from 1985 is analyzed. The research utilized data from the IUE to model the star's spectrum during the flare. A comparison of models revealed that the flare's spectrum was composed of two components - an extremely hot, compact core and a surrounding, hotter layer of swirling gas. This analysis also demonstrated that the standard model of an accretion shock, with the accretion occurring above 1 million Kelvin, could accurately fit the data in the ultraviolet range. However, this study found that the model was unable to account for the observed optical flux during the flare. It was found that the flare's optical excess could be explained by a cooler, higher layer of gas at around 20,000 Kelvin. This finding suggests that the geometry of the star's flare is more complex than previously thought, with multiple layers of gas at different temperatures contributing to the observed spectrum. This research provides new insights into the physics of stellar flares and the importance of accurately modeling the continuum during spectroscopic analysis. It is also demonstrated that the conventional methods for measuring the flux of a star during a flare may lead to an underestimation of the flare's true magnitude. This study highlights the value of archival data in contributing to our understanding of high-energy events on active stars. It is recommended that future research instruments for studying stellar flares give due consideration to the importance of continuum modeling. This study's findings have implications for the search for biosignatures in the spectra of exoplanets, with potential high-energy events on these planets potentially masking the signals of life. It is also noted that the techniques employed in this study could be adapted for use with the upcoming STAMINA spectrograph. often overlooked in static settings. This paper introduces a novel novel high-
rank embedding framework that leverages temporal relations and constraints found
within time-stamped triples in a knowledge graph. This framework is characterized
by two key features: (1) time-agnostic representations are utilized to capture the
underlying properties and concepts of entities and (2) time-specific relations are
defined to describe the temporal connections between entities. This novel approach
is model-agnostic, allowing it to be integrated with existing graph embedding
techniques. We evaluate our proposed method in conjunction with three popular

knowledge graph benchmark datasets. Notably, our method demonstrates a notable
reduction in model size while maintaining competitive performance when compared

achieves the best balance between high performance and the risk of overfitting. This
advantage is particularly pronounced when modeling high-dimensional temporal
knowledge graphs. We believe that this research contributes meaningfully to the

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. Furthermore, a case study is conducted to examine the relationship between physically extracted clusters and the proposed algorithm's results, highlighting the approach's potential to provide a data-driven alternative to influence-based clustering in complex systems. This data-driven approach is also compared to traditional spectral clustering methods, revealing that it yields more robust results in line with theoretical expectations. This comparison also demonstrates the ability of the proposed algorithm to recover linear and non-linear communities, thus it can be a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners in various fields and can be easily integrated into existing clustering pipelines.
