We have investigated the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN thin films, which exhibit a unique magnetic structure due to long-range magnetic interactions. Our research reveals that a strong thermomagnetic voltage generates an unusual, asymmetric response in these films, particularly in regions away from magnetic transitions. Moreover, we found that the anomalous Nernst coefficient is directly proportional to the specific heat of the material and shows minimal variation with increased magnetic field strength. Our findings suggest that the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN can be understood through a combination of the Seebeck effect and magnetic structure changes. Lastly, we observed a significant enhancement of the anomalous Nernst effect when these films undergo a phase transition from the A-phase to the B-phase. Notably, the B-phase exhibits greater thermomagnetic voltage in both direction and magnitude compared to the A-phase. This increase in the anomalous Nernst effect during the A to B phase transition in Mn$_3$NiN films may have significant implications for their use in magnetic cooling applications. The core of PILE lies in a novel pairwise iterative logits ensemble algorithm, which utilizes unlabeled data to refine the student's logits and produce a probability distribution. These refined logits are then used to adjust the weights of the models during the autodidact learning phase. The proposed framework is mathematically analyzed to ensure its convergence. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks (GNNs), have successfully tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing the underlying connectivity structure of datasets. However, real-world data often exhibits changing connectivity patterns over time, a phenomenon not addressed by conventional static GNN approaches. To bridge this gap, we developed a novel neural network method called Deep Dynamic Effective Connectivity Estimation (DDECE), which simultaneously models both node interactions and their temporal evolution. By utilizing this model's dynamic representation of connectivity, we improve classification performance on time-series classification tasks. Experimental results show that this dynamic representation yields a 10% improvement in accuracy on the NMI metric when compared to static approaches, and a notable 50% reduction in error rate on certain datasets. Furthermore, DDECE's links and node representations are interpretable, enabling us to identify newly formed connections as well as those that disappeared over time. In contrast to traditional methods, we also introduce a novel evaluation metric called the Half Life Index (HLI), which assesses the dynamic performance of models on datasets with changing graph structures. Overall, our results demonstrate the superiority of DDECE over conventional methods in capturing and utilizing the temporal variations in graph data. Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can be used to validate results or inform Bayesian analysis. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a range of phylogenetic network generators by evaluating and contrasting the topological characteristics of the generated networks as a function of the number of reticulations present. This evaluation helps us gauge the accuracy of each generator in reproducing the expected distribution of tree topologies and informs our understanding of the relationship between the number of reticulations and the resulting network topology. Our study comprises a thorough examination of 13 different network generators capable of producing binary networks containing up to four reticulations. The results reveal significant disparities in the topological characteristics of generated networks, with some matching the expected distribution of tree topologies while others deviate significantly. Moreover, our findings indicate that the relationship between the number of reticulations and resulting network topology is not always straightforward, underscoring the complexity involved in modeling phylogenetic networks through graph-theoretic structures. Ultimately, our research underscores the importance of transparent publication of generation tools, along with accessible implementation and data to facilitate comparison and validation of such methods. This study paves the way for a broader examination of the relationship between graph structures and phylogenetic networks, an area with applications in phylogeny reconstruction, network inference, and comparative genomics. The iterative matrix inversion method offers a promising solution to accelerate matrix inversion, particularly for large Hermitian positive-definite matrices commonly encountered in linear systems, neutron transport, electromagnetic scattering, and eigenvalue problems. By analyzing the cost of each accelerated iteration and comparing it to the cost of a direct inversion using a given sparse solver, we derive a general formula to estimate the speedup achievable with each method. This formulation enables the selection of the method that yields the maximum possible speedup given the available GPU memory. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these accelerated methods on a range of large eigenvalue problems and demonstrate that they can deliver substantial speedups on a GPU, with improvements ranging from one order of magnitude to several orders of magnitude. Furthermore, we show that the optimal accelerated method may not provide a working solution, highlighting the importance of introducing a fallback strategy to ensure a usable solution can be obtained. By employing this strategy, we achieve accelerated solutions on a significantly larger dataset of 10,000 eigenvalues. The PHENIX Collaboration has obtained novel direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions from 2006 to 2011, enabling precise assessments of jet-medium interactions. These findings reveal that the hadron yield around the jet axis is significantly reduced in Au$+$Au compared to $d$$+$Au, with little change in hadron momentum and type. This result indicates the jet is efficiently coupled with the medium to produce bulk hadron production, particularly for hadrons with low momentum. Furthermore, hadron tracks at large angles to the jet (opposite to the jet direction) exhibit reduced yields in Au$+$Au, indicating the jet's ability to interact with the medium across a significant distance. These findings are consistent with the idea that jets transfer energy to the medium through multiple medium interactions, with significant implications for our understanding of jet-medium interactions. These results also highlight the need for models that describe jet energy loss to account for hadron production outside the jet's initial interaction with the medium. Additionally, hadron tracks at large angles to the jet in $d$$+$Au fall above baseline levels, suggesting that hadron production in this region may be influenced by the impact parameter, glancing binary collisions, or the interaction of hadrons with underlying nucleons, underscoring the importance of studying jet-medium interactions in peripheral hadron collisions. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of jet-medium interactions and the behavior of quark-gluon plasmas under extreme conditions. A fundamental challenge in robotics and animal locomotion research is addressing how non-rigid terrain affects legged robots' movement. Effective communication through language inevitably involves handling contradictions, contradictions that are explicitly expressed through negation. Although a fundamental aspect of language, negation's intricacies pose significant challenges to language models, particularly their ability to accurately capture the implications of negation during question answering. In an effort to address these limitations, we introduce CONDAQA, a novel English question answering dataset that requires answers to be based on understanding the negation of a paragraph in order to arrive at the correct conclusion. This dataset consists of 13,872 human-annotated pairs of paragraphs and answers, with a specific focus on the implications of negation. We introduce CONDAQAQA, a strong baseline model that achieves 61.1% in matching the original answer's semantics, but falls to 26.6% in matching the answer's surface form. This represents a significant gap, indicating that models struggle to capture the implications of negation during question answering. Notably, we find that the performance of models is heavily influenced by their ability to grasp the negation's semantic implications. As a result, improving the semantic understanding of negation will likely have a critical impact on future advancements in this dataset. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we've developed a novel approach to generating hierarchies that utilizes word embeddings and latent Dirichlet allocation, allowing us to model networks as interconnected topics and leverage a hierarchical structure to reduce computational costs. By applying this method to the LDA model, we've created an efficient algorithm that can accurately construct hierarchies and the underlying distribution of topics without having to distribute models across multiple machines. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of this method by applying it to the Wikipedia category network, resulting in a significant improvement in computing time and a validation of the generated hierarchies through user feedback. The resulting models also exhibit a higher level of consistency, with fewer topics that are isolated or difficult to interpret. Furthermore, this approach enables easier navigation by identifying natural abstraction levels and reducing the complexity of the hierarchy without sacrificing critical information. Quantum annealing within the framework of quantum simulation offers a promising path for tackling intractable combinatorial optimization problems. This approach involves mapping the problem into an Ising Hamiltonian that can be solved using quantum Monte Carlo simulation. However, the success of this method relies heavily on the quality of the quantum annealing protocol. A crucial factor influencing this outcome is the 'quantum annealing gap', which represents the difference between ground states at the beginning and end points of the protocol. A large quantum annealing gap indicates a more complex quench dynamics, which in turn may hinder the Monte Carlo simulation's efficiency in solving the problem. This paper investigates the quantum annealing gap and quench dynamics in the context of the exact cover problem, which has significant applications in computer science and machine learning. By analyzing the impact of cavity field strengths and nearest-neighbor couplings on quench dynamics and quantum annealing gap, this study reveals that increasing these interactions can actually impede the problem-solving process. This counterintuitive finding may seem at odds with the generally held assumption that larger interactions between quantum spins would facilitate successful quantum annealing. This research highlights the importance of meticulously examining the quench dynamics and quantum annealing gap for each specific problem, rather than relying on general principles. This knowledge can be used to optimize quantum annealing protocols, even in cases where the mapping to an Ising Hamiltonian model involves cavity spins. This approach could be particularly useful in combining quantum annealing with other simulation model mappings. This paper's findings also suggest that there are benefits to using a quantum annealing protocol that involves a series of gradual changes in parameters, rather than a single sudden quench. This insight can be applied to solve complex computational problems by leveraging the interplay between quantum and classical dynamics. We re-examined the wave-slope statistics of Cox and Munk (1954) using infrared radiation data from space, which directly observe the sea surface, and found their results to be misleading due to the method of data averaging they used. When we averaged their data correctly, we found the distribution of wave slopes to be in line with a theoretical model that assumes waves are randomly oriented, and the relationship between wave slope and solar elevation was much weaker than Cox and Munk found, which has implications for estimating solar radiation entering the ocean. This average distribution of wave slopes is now more accurate and could be used in calculations of solar radiation and other related phenomena. 

This revised distribution differs from the original findings of Cox and Munk in several ways: their data was based on images of the sea taken from a satellite, which may not have accurately captured the distribution of wave slopes over the entire ocean, and their method of analyzing the data led to an overestimation of the impact of solar elevation on wave slopes. 

We also found that using the revised distribution of wave slopes results in a more accurate calculation of solar radiation entering the ocean, especially when the solar elevation is low. This has implications for the validation of models that estimate this radiation, and highlights the importance of using the most accurate data available when validating such models against observations. 

This revised distribution of wave slopes could also be useful in other contexts where it is used, and we recommend that it be adopted in place of the original results of Cox and Munk to ensure the most accurate results possible.

We collected and analyzed the ISB-Covid19 dataset, containing 10,000 Hindi tweets, and evaluated the effectiveness of various machine learning models, including decision trees, support vector machines, and long short-term memory networks. Our experiments revealed that the LSTM model delivered the most accurate results, outperforming traditional models by a significant margin. Initially, the Lawrence-Doniach and interlayer tunneling models were the prominent theoretical concepts to describe cuprate superconductors by connecting CuO planes through Josephson coupling. However, the discovery of larger than predicted interlayer magnetic penetration depths in these materials led to the resurgence of interest in the Lawrence-Doniach model. This resurgence was further fueled by the appearance of charge density waves (CDWs) in some cuprates, which potentially align with superconducting domains. Consequently, this resurgence led to the assumption that CDWs could be viewed as alternate layers, enabling the generalization of the Lawrence-Doniach model to describe superconducting properties in cuprates with charge density waves. This generalized model can be seen as an extension of the interlayer tunneling model, where Josephson coupling is replaced by coupling between superconducting and charge density wave order parameters within adjacent layers. This new model can be used to interpret the observed phenomena in YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{7-x}$, such as the relationship between superconducting and charge density wave transition temperatures, as well as the effects of magnetic field on superconducting and charge density wave order parameters. This generalized model also highlights the significance of considering the interaction between superconducting and charge density wave layers in understanding the superconducting properties of materials with coexisting orders. This concept is further supported by the similarity between the ratio of interlayer magnetic penetration depths and the ratio of the costs of condensation free energies for superconducting and charge density wave orders, which is consistent with the predictions of the generalized model. This discovery underscores the importance of examining the relationship between superconducting and charge density wave orders in materials with coexisting orders, which can provide valuable insights into the understanding of superconducting phenomena. This perspective piece discusses the implications of this generalized model for future experimental and theoretical studies of superconducting materials with charge density waves. This perspective piece also includes a discussion on the implications of this generalized model for the concept of superfluidity, which may be relevant for future studies on superconducting materials with charge density waves. The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are not yet fully understood and may influence neutron star dynamics and gravitational waves.  This study investigates how the velocity of sound in such matter is affected by various interactions and the types of quarks present, particularly in contexts where quantum anomalies of dense matter lead to instability in neutron star models.  By analyzing the conditions necessary for stable, non-rotating compact stars at densities between neutron star and quark star densities, this research identifies ranges of parameters that can lead to stable models of strange compact stars and provides constraints on the velocity of sound in these stars.  It is found that the velocity of sound in such matter must be below the maximum value of approximately 1.73 times the velocity of light in nuclear vacuum conditions to allow for stable dense matter states.  This research also offers parameter ranges for compact stars composed of dense, non-strange nuclear matter and strangeness, and could serve as a basis for further studies into the fundamental properties of compact stars.  This study is also conducted using a phenomenological approach, with the velocity of sound determined by the density of strange quark condensates rather than quark flavors.  This could provide a starting point for more detailed studies into the properties of dense matter within compact stars.  This research is relevant to the scientific goals of future high precision multi-messenger astrophysics involving compact stars and black holes. This paper proposes a new concept, Anti Tai Mapping, which is a one-to-one correspondence between the leaves of two input trees. We then demonstrate that Anti Tai Mapping is invariant under the presence of reticulations or unknown tree topologies, thereby providing a valuable tool for comparative genomic studies. Furthermore, this new concept is closely related to the notion of Maximum Agreement Forest, and we explore its connection to this forest type. We have thoroughly tested this algorithm's efficacy on a diverse range of benchmark datasets. The concept of a hidden trait, or backdoor, in machine learning models has gained significance in recent years, as it refers to a feature that affects their decision-making process and is triggered by specific input data. Backdoors can be particularly problematic in settings where model outputs significantly impact users' lives. Research has made progress in identifying and mitigating static backdoors that remain constant throughout a model's operation. However, the field still lacks a clear understanding of dynamic backdoors that change as the input data evolves. This study aims to bridge this knowledge gap by introducing a new theory that explains how dynamic backdoors work and identifying a specific pattern, global average pooling, that characterizes them. It also shows that models incorporating global average pooling are prone to developing a type of temporal backdoor triggered by continuous input signals. To address this issue, it proposes a method to detect temporal backdoors by analyzing a model's behavior across different time points. Moreover, it demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in identifying both static and temporal backdoors. Finally, it discusses the potential for generalizing this solution to other types of models and highlights the importance of further research in this area. This research is an important step towards developing more robust machine learning models that are less susceptible to hidden flaws. It is crucial to recognize that this work is preliminary and future studies will be necessary to fully explore the concepts introduced here. In particular, the paper raises questions about the relationship between temporal backdoors and other issues such as data poisoning and the reliability of models that make predictions over time. It also proposes a new definition for temporal backdoors and suggests methods for testing whether a model has developed a temporal backdoor. However, these ideas will need to be refined and validated through additional experiments. In summary, this study is an attempt to lay the groundwork for a deeper understanding of dynamic backdoors and to explore ways to identify and mitigate this type of issue. It is essential to emphasize that this research is in its early stages, and more work will be necessary to fully address these concepts. Analyzing the impact of general relativity on Gaia-like astrometry, we've determined that deviations from Newton's law become negligible at a distance of several thousand parsecs from the system's center of mass. As a result, the uncertainty in the gravitational potential's PPN gamma parameter has a negligible effect on astrometric measurements for objects with masses typically found on such celestial bodies. However, the uncertainty in gamma does have a detectable influence on the estimated luminosity of stars, amounting to 0.1 microarcseconds. This effect is comparable to the improvement in parallax measurements resulting from a 10% reduction in Gaia's photometric noise. Consequently, the most significant improvement in parallax accuracy will stem from reducing systematic errors in photometry. The concept of self-accelerating solitons was first introduced in 2007 in a paper by J. K. Abusupyan, R. Adams, and S. J. Singh, published in the journal "Physical Review A". This work built upon a previous finding by Singh and co-authors, which revealed that an effective model for Bose-Einstein condensates, described by a mean-field Gross-Pitaevskii equation, could exhibit persistent, zero-momentum soliton solutions in the presence of a nonvanishing magnetic field. However, the original paper lacked a clear, comprehensive explanation for the observed self-trapping phenomenon. In a series of theoretical simulations, we re-examined this phenomenon, uncovering new insights and generalizations. By applying a discrete-momentum approximation to simulate nonlinear dipole modes in one-dimensional Bose-Josephson systems, we successfully demonstrated the self-trapping feature in both harmonic potential and trapping barriers, and found that it is robust against changes in the strength of the nonlinear interaction. Furthermore, we found that the ratio of the self-trapped peak heights to the initial value is proportional to the square of the ratio of the magnetic field to the nonlinear interaction, providing a universal scaling relationship that applies universally to both discrete and continuous models. Additionally, we explored the dynamics of self-trapping in one-dimensional Bose-Josephson systems, revealing that the feature persists even in the presence of gaps, and uncovering a new condition for self-trapping, characterized by the number of junctions, the strength of the nonlinear interaction, and the size of the gap. In the case of two- and three-dimensional systems, we found that the self-trapping feature is more challenging to achieve due to the greater tendency of these systems to fragment into multiple peaks. However, we successfully demonstrated self-trapping in these dimensions using a combination of beam and magnetic field, and showed that the self-trapping ratio can be controlled by adjusting the intensity of the beam. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge can be problematical, as it may introduce irrelevant knowledge, leading to inaccurate answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic graph-based knowledge-aware question answering approach, which prioritizes the incorporation of background knowledge on a question-by-question basis. Initially, we construct a semantic graph based on the question's semantics, which allows us to filter potentially relevant knowledge. In the subsequent stage, we gradually incorporate more knowledge into the graph, refining the knowledge with increasing precision. The knowledge is evaluated based on the question's semantics, ensuring that only semantically related knowledge is incorporated. We test our approach on the CommonsenseQA dataset and achieve notable improvements over strong baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of our strategy in selecting and utilizing background knowledge. Furthermore, we highlight the general applicability of our approach to other open-domain question answering tasks. We also introduce a semantic graph evaluation metric, along with a new dataset named Commonsense Graph Data (CGD), which provides gold-standard semantic graphs for each question. These innovations contribute significantly to the field of open-domain question answering. The code and data are available at https://github.com/zheng-xy/Coarse2Careful. For more information, please refer to the technical paper available at arXiv:2206.08234. Additionally, a video presentation can be found at https://youtu.be/6Q5s6L9I6FQ. We have also conducted a survey on the difficulty of Commonsense Graph Data, releasing the dataset and the results at https://github.com/zheng-xy/CommonsenseGraphDifficulty. Moreover, we have released a new dataset named Commonsense Graph Data with Answers (CGDA), along with the code and data at https://github.com/zheng-xy/CommonsenseGraphDataWithAnswers. We hope that these contributions will advance the study of open-domain question answering and graph-based knowledge-aware question answering. By utilizing pyKT, researchers can ensure the fairness of comparisons involving deep learning-based models, and the library's modular structure allows for easy integration of new models, evaluation methods, and dataset assets. The development of standardized benchmarks using pyKT is expected to promote more effective model evaluations and facilitate the exploration of approaches to improve knowledge tracing through generalization, by making the source code and benchmark results openly available. We have established the pyKT platform with three deep learning-based knowledge tracing challenge datasets, spanning English and math topics, and have conducted a thorough analysis of the generalization performance of various models on these benchmarks. The results indicate that the best models are highly dependent on the specific dataset, highlighting the significance of generalization in knowledge tracing and providing the community with the opportunity to explore this aspect further. The pyKT library and the associated results are available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyangwang/pyKT. One notable aspect of pyKT is its emphasis on transparent reporting, which follows the guidelines set forth by the Machine Learning Reproducibility Consortium. Despite advancements in end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition, achieving high accuracy across various languages and conditions remains a significant challenge. To overcome this, we propose a novel two-stage transcription method that leverages advanced models. Initially, a simple neural network quickly generates a coarse transcript from the audio, drawing on a diverse pool of training data that includes transcriptions derived from models tailored to similar languages. For each word in the coarse transcript, we retrieve a short list of possible refinements. Ultimately, the refined words are selected through a combination of the coarse transcript's language model and acoustic scores. We demonstrate that this approach yields a significant improvement in data efficiency and transcribes utterances with a 20% lower word error rate in cross-lingual scenarios and 15% in noisy environments, compared to standard neural networks. Furthermore, we show that this method facilitates seamless adaptation to new languages with just a few annotated examples. We also explore the benefits of pre-training the coarse network on unsupervised transcriptions and propose a novel strategy for selecting similar languages in cross-lingual scenarios based on the phonetic distance between languages. We validate our approach through a range of experiments in 10 languages. We anticipate that this method will be particularly useful for low-resource languages and scenarios involving a significant amount of background noise. This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the minimal number of comparators required to sort n distinct values, where each comparator combines the values in some order and rearranges them to be in non-decreasing order. We investigate constant-depth sorting networks, those with a fixed small number of layers, as they provide insight into the fundamental structure of sorting networks. In particular, we identify a family of constant-depth sorting networks with depth d, consisting of d layers, that sorts n values using the minimum number of comparators among all d-layer sorting networks. We establish an upper bound of approximately n^2/ (d^2 - d) comparators for the d-layer networks, and this bound is achievable for sufficiently large n values. Additionally, we discuss lower bounds for constant-depth sorting networks, including an lower bound of approximately 0.5n^2 comparators for single-layer networks, which improves upon our previous publication. Furthermore, we introduce a lower bound for d-layer networks of approximately 0.5n^2 / (d^2 - d) comparators, and this lower bound applies across all d values. Notably, we discovered constant-depth sorting networks that use a significantly smaller number of comparators than the well-known construction method using recursive digital sorting networks. We found that the recursive digital sorting networks have a comparator structure that is highly similar to the structure of binary sorting networks, and we found this similarity to be the key factor that led to the similar upper bounds for both the binary and the recursive digital sorting networks. In contrast, the constant-depth sorting networks we identified have a comparator structure that is significantly different from both the binary and the recursive digital sorting networks, and this difference led to a significant reduction in the number of comparators required. This discovery suggests that the concept of sorting networks is rich and diverse, and further research is needed to fully understand its structure. This study explores how uncertainty about chance influencing job success and earnings impacts redistribution policies in a diverse group of people. These findings have implications for research aiming to model people's opinions on income inequality and the apparent disparity between laboratory research and real-world inequality trends in the US. We suggest that laboratory research may not fully capture how people perceive the relationship between luck and income inequality. We also identify areas for further research into how people view the concept of luck in relation to income inequality. The concept of single-particle entanglement is often misunderstood, with some researchers believing it's equivalent to non-locality as seen in Bell's inequality tests. However, true non-locality, such as single-particle steering, cannot arise from single-particle entanglement alone. Our study shows that in order to see non-local effects like single-particle steering, a system must be bi-entangled, meaning that there is an entanglement between two particles, and we demonstrate this using a simple example with photons. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable or is complicated in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign. Therefore, we employ an alternative strategy based on an expanded energy functional, specifically designed to account for the terms generated by boundary singularities. This approach enables us to transform the problem into a quasi-variational inequality problem, ultimately allowing us to recover the optimal blow-up criterion. This research is a significant extension of our previous work on this issue in reference [9]. Similar results have also been achieved for Dirac equations with mass-supercritical nonlinearities. By linking quantum error correcting codes to models of disordered classical statistical mechanics and applying the concepts of droplet formation and percolation, we explore the origins of fault tolerance in realistic circuit architectures. We examine how variations in quantum gate execution and readout affect performance, focusing on two commonly used codes: topological quantum codes and stabilizer codes without topology. Our analysis reveals that the stability of these codes depends crucially on the relationship between two fundamental thresholds: the quantum circuit threshold and the classical decoding threshold. A gap between these thresholds indicates that the quantum system can maintain accuracy despite errors, while their convergence marks the onset of system failure. We investigate various scenarios of quantum gate failure and readout in rotation and phase codes, finding distinct effects of gate type and whether failures in one gate correlate with those in another. Notably, failure rotation has a significant impact on performance, reducing the classical decoding threshold and thus the gap between thresholds, while still increasing the circuit threshold, thus complicating fault diagnosis. The influence of readout on performance is found to be less significant, merging with the rotation case for large error rates. A notable feature of our study is the use of classical quenched averaging, which standard simulation techniques cannot efficiently explore large gaps between thresholds. This allowed us to examine thresholds for codes that fail completely under standard simulation methods. This knowledge of thresholds, combined with an understanding of how quantum systems fail, could guide the selection of quantum gates and readout methods for optimal performance in real-world quantum computing applications. This research is also relevant to other areas of quantum computing beyond error correction, such as reliable quantum control and measurement of systems subject to fluctuations. Furthermore, the insights gained from this study on the importance of fundamental thresholds could be applied to other areas of complex systems where the interplay between order and disorder gives rise to phase transitions. This includes systems of quantum systems, such as spin glasses in magnetic fields and phase transitions in quantum annealing, where similar concepts of droplet formation and percolation apply. We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method utilizes traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent approach for blocking fractures. This strategy enables the use of traditional $h$-pdiscontinuous Galerkin methods for conductive fractures while allowing the introduction of non-conservative terms to account for flow across blocking fractures. This approach is then applied to a variety of test cases, including examples of conductive and blocking fractures in both 2D and 3D settings. Our results demonstrate that this method is capable of handling a wide range of fracture permeability ratios, producing accurate and convergent numerical solutions. This paper provides a theoretical framework for this method and presents a range of numerical implementations. Furthermore, it highlights potential improvements, such as further investigation of time-dependent problems and development of more robust fracture mesh generators. This research is an initial step towards developing a more comprehensive numerical model that can effectively simulate Darcy flow within complex fractured porous media. This model has the potential to be integrated with other models, such as those for oil reservoir simulation. This is because single-phase Darcy flow is a fundamental component of many multiphase flow applications, including oil and gas reservoir simulation. A comprehensive examination of a spin-triplet superconducting device, which involves a spiral magnetic arrangement, is conducted to determine its operation in two distinct scenarios: a uniformly magnetized device and one with a distinct valve function.  The underlying material properties are investigated for each scenario, with particular focus on the paramagnetic and orbital interference effects.  The results indicate that the device can effectively operate as a valve even in the absence of magnetic order, under specific conditions that align with the superconducting pair structure.  The study also reveals that the device's performance can be influenced by both magnetic domains and crystal imperfections, introducing possible challenges for the realization of this concept.  A proposed design that incorporates a chiral domain structure is suggested as an approach to overcome these difficulties.  The study provides a foundation for exploring the device's capabilities in the presence of magnetic fields and temperature.  The proposed design may also offer a pathway to enhancing the device's performance.  The study is further applicable to the study of superconducting spin-triplet devices in general. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a specific Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex; (2) it has a unique local minimum in an appropriately defined neighborhood; (3) it exhibits an infinite number of local minima elsewhere. Additionally, we analyze the generalization capabilities of this type of optimization problem when the objective function f is an empirical risk minimization. Under the assumption that f satisfies a growth condition, we show that an exponentially large number of distinct local minima of the factorized version occurs with probability one as the sample size increases. The results further indicate that such methods are inherently prone to overfitting and that existing works that analyze the landscape of matrix factorization are limited to a specific local regime. A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors. This new example is particularly notable as it is the first known instance of a bipartite cubic graph that is not strongly edge colorable. This new example contradicts multiple previous approaches that attempted to resolve the conjecture originally presented by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990. Moreover, this new example also provides strong evidence that in general, no generalised bound exists for the number of colours needed to strongly edge colour any graph, even considering graphs that are bipartite and have a high enough girth. This new example can be described using a specific construction method, but this construction method creates graphs that are not minimal, which in turn means that in the future, research will be needed to determine if there are any graphs that are minimal and require a certain number of colours to be strongly edge coloured. This paper will present analytic expressions for $L(2k,\chi)$ and $L(2k,-1)$ in integer form, where these identities connect L-functions with properties of prime numbers, revealing links between the zeros of L-functions and the behavior of prime numbers. This research could also provide insights for the study of natural swimmers, like bacteria and sperm cells, which often have asymmetrical structures. By exploring different materials and designs, our study can help find the optimal combination for achieving high swimming speeds in both forward and backward directions. This is especially important because many natural swimmers rely on swimming backward to change direction. Our study consists of both theoretical and experimental components, using both simulations and actual swimmers made from different materials to test our hypotheses. This research can contribute to the advancement of bio-inspired robotics and might provide insights into the swimming mechanics of living organisms. Our analysis revealed that the outcome of these algorithms consistently corresponds to the socially optimal output levels, which is characterized by the product of two marginal costs under perfect competition. This result demonstrates that, regardless of the specific cost functions, the Nash equilibrium in a duopoly Cournot game will not resemble the outcome of perfect competition. Furthermore, we observed that the emergence of a Nash equilibrium in these models is dependent on the design of the search space. If the ability to search for optimal outcomes is limited, the resulting output levels may instead converge to those that yield the highest profits for each individual firm, rather than reaching the Nash equilibrium. This finding is supported by an additional experiment involving three firms, which showed that the product of two marginal costs remains a suitable indicator of the socially optimal output levels even in a triopoly Cournot game. This outcome suggests that the simplicity of this indicator makes it particularly useful for visualizing the search space in a manner that facilitates the discovery of the socially optimal output levels. This, in turn, implies that firms facing substantial search costs may still fail to establish a Nash equilibrium in a Cournot game. This research contributes to the ongoing debate regarding the existence of endogenous mechanisms that can generate a Nash equilibrium in a reasonable timeframe. Our results indicate that the notion of firms being patient and able to reach a Nash equilibrium through a process of trial and error is plausible. This research also highlights the potential benefits of employing co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in conjunction with computational social science. By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, given that we choose the model that best fits observational data through the Bayesian Information Criterion. Furthermore, even using a line that is more susceptible to dust effects, we find that the predictions are still accurate, at least for galaxies at relatively close distances. We also find that the relationship between the observed and predicted values of this line is independent of the method used to determine star formation rates, and that it differs from the relationship found for another line. This suggests that while different methods of estimating star formation rates may have different advantages and disadvantages, they are all capable of accurately capturing the overall relationship between this line and star formation rates.

Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry algorithms have been developed to estimate positions using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These algorithms have particularly shown great potential for use with consumer-grade devices. However, the limited computational power of these devices means that processing raw sensor data is impractical, and thus preprocessing is necessary to reduce the data dimensionality. In this context, we propose a new external memory attention-based framework, EMA-VIO, for visual-inertial odometry that can handle preprocessed feature maps, effectively addressing the pose estimation challenge. By utilizing an external memory to focus on relevant information and integrate it with recurrent poses, our framework achieves superior performance, surpassing state-of-the-art VIO results in the TUM-VIO and EuRoC megamixed datasets. Moreover, EMA-VIO's efficiency in the deep learning approach makes it highly suitable for use with mobile devices. Code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/EMA-VIO. In particular, our results show that EMA-VIO outperforms VIO-Sync and DVO in terms of ADE, and achieves comparable performance to traditional VIO methods using raw data, while being significantly more efficient and accurate with real-world datasets. Moreover, our analysis of attention maps provides valuable insights into the proposed external memory attention mechanism. In particular, we find that the attention mechanism can effectively capture the motion pattern, and the reasons for its improved performance, and we also demonstrate the general applicability of the external memory attention framework to VIO. Finally, we discuss potential directions for future research in this area. Furthermore, we introduce a new dataset, the VIO dataset, which consists of 10 challenging sequences, and is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/EMA-VIO. In contrast to active young stars, solar-like stars exhibit minimal or no external magnetic activity. These low-activity stars typically rotate slowly, and their rotation rates often indicate a limited differential rotation. Since the differential rotation in these stars has a reversed polarity, known as anti-solar differential rotation, it could potentially impact the type of dynamo that operates within them. This reversal of differential rotation may alter the symmetry of the differential rotation and the associated alpha-effect, possibly inhibiting the generation of large-scale poloidal magnetic field and limiting magnetic cycles in these stars. To investigate this possibility, we employ the ProxyDynAS scheme, which models the nonlinear interaction between rotation, convection, and magnetic field generation, and applies it to a range of solar-like stars with anti-solar differential rotation. According to our simulations, the reduction in differential rotation amplifies the toroidal magnetic field generated by the alpha-effect, potentially leading to magnetic field buildup in these stars. This buildup may contribute to the observed correlations between slow rotators' magnetic fields and rotation rates. Furthermore, our simulations suggest that the occurrence of magnetic cycles in these stars is rotation rate-dependent, with cycles more likely in stars with rotation rates above 1.5 times the estimated solar rotation rate. This study highlights the significance of considering the impact of anti-solar differential rotation on the dynamo process in solar-like stars, particularly in their outer convective zones. It also emphasizes the need for observational constraints on their rotation rates and magnetic fields to better understand the operation of dynamos in these low-activity stars. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the search for hidden magnetic cycles in these stars, and the potential for magnetic cycles to influence their magnetic field properties. Additionally, we outline the potential for future research to be guided by the predictions made in this study. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws that cause degradation and limit the effectivity of these systems. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric properties and structural integrity of resonators within superconducting quantum integral interferometry circuits. We also observed the effect of chemical mechanical polishing on these issues, finding that it removes impurities while introducing surface defects that can be managed through optimized processing. Furthermore, we believe this approach can be applied to the study and improvement of other complex quantum systems. Additionally, we have made the sample preparation process more efficient by developing a method to pattern superconducting materials using a dry process, eliminating the need for lithography and its associated polymer layers. This has allowed us to achieve low loss rates in resonators without the need for near-field analysis. This breakthrough has significant implications for the development of practical quantum systems. While convolutional neural networks excel in medical image segmentation, their performance is often hindered by limited data and inconsistencies between training and testing images. Semi-supervised learning has shown promise in addressing these challenges by adaptively transferring knowledge across similar anatomical structures with limited labeled data. This approach is particularly appealing because it allows for the extraction of feature representations from unannotated images during training. However, the traditional method of extracting feature representations results in the loss of patient-specific information, which is critical for segmenting similar structures. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel contrastive semi-supervised learning framework that leverages both unlabeled and labeled images to capture both universal and patient-specific feature representations. This framework involves two main components: first, a contrastive encoder is used to extract universal feature representations from both labeled and unannotated images by comparing encoded segments; second, a transfer encoder is employed to transfer the universal representations to the unannotated images. We evaluate our proposed framework on two publicly available datasets, demonstrating its superiority over the baseline models and the benefits of incorporating a contrastive encoder and transfer encoder. Furthermore, our results indicate that this framework achieves comparable performance to expert-drawn ground truth and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in cross-domain segmentation. Additionally, our code and guidelines for conducting thorough ablation studies are available for download. This framework has the potential to become a go-to method for medical image segmentation tasks. This research provides a foundation for exploring other applications of contrastive learning in medical imaging. Kopczyński (ICALP 2006) hypothesized that prefix-independence in half-positional winning conditions leads to closed unions. Contrary to this hypothesis, we demonstrate that such conditions are not finite union-closed over general game histories. To achieve this counterexample, we expand on previous work by extending half-positional winning conditions to competitive reachability games on totally ordered graphs, thus showing that conditions of this type are not closed under finite unions. This development builds upon previous research utilizing modified objective functions and extended tree orders. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the underlying structure of the game graph contributes significantly to the characteristics of winning conditions. As a result, we can create a new set of half-positional winning conditions for any given game graph, even though the union of individual conditions within this set would not result in a half-positional condition. This counterexample provides evidence that the concept of prefix-independence is crucial for ensuring the closure of unions of positional winning conditions. Additionally, we introduce the notion of a condition being 'first-move winning' and prove that all half-positional conditions are indeed first-move winning. However, we also demonstrate that not all first-move winning conditions are half-positional. Finally, we explore alternative definitions of half-positional winning conditions and show that these definitions are equivalent to the original definition used in this research. This includes defining half-positional winning conditions using the notion of a 'position tree', which is a tree in which the leaf nodes represent game positions. This concept further solidifies the connection between game history and tree structures. Lastly, we discuss potential applications of these findings to other types of games and potential research avenues. This includes examining whether similar counterexamples can be found in games with multiple winners or in games where the order of the player order is not fixed. Additionally, we discuss the concept of extending half-positional conditions to more complex game structures and the idea of exploring other definitions of half-positional conditions. This could involve defining half-positional conditions using the notion of a 'position tree' or by considering whether a winning condition is half-positional if it only depends on the current position and the previous position. This could potentially lead to new insights into the characteristics of half-positional conditions. The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their orbital period. The detection rate of these systems in soft X-ray bands is notably low compared to their non-asynchronous counterparts, which has led to the speculation that asynchronous polars might exhibit distinct accretion patterns. In this study, we conducted a comparison of the X-ray hardness ratios of non-asynchronous polars and asynchronous polars using data from the XMM-Newton observatory, with the aim of identifying any differences in spectral behavior between these two categories. Our analysis revealed no statistical difference in hardness ratios between non-asynchronous polars and asynchronous polars, contradicting the initial hypothesis that the latter exhibit distinct accretion patterns. This finding suggests that the low detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft X-ray bands might be attributed to other factors, such as the systems' geometric properties or the orientation of their accretion axes. This study further emphasizes the importance of considering all subtypes of polars in any analysis of their collective behavior. For mobile robots to effectively navigate in unfamiliar surroundings, it is crucial to have a robust mapping system that can adapt to any environment. Current mapping techniques often rely on two-dimensional representations, such as occupancy grids or pose graphs, but these methods fail to capture the topology of the space, a fundamental concept that has been well established in animal navigation for centuries. To address this limitation, we propose a novel mapping framework called HiTMap, which utilizes a topological map to represent the space and a hierarchical structure to facilitate navigation. By leveraging HiTMap's topology and a navigation function based on local pose graphs, we demonstrate significant improvements in navigation accuracy and efficiency compared to non-hierarchical approaches. Moreover, we evaluate the performance of HiTMap on a simulation scenario and a real-world experiment, showcasing its ability to create a reliable and navigable map in a short time frame. The resulting map allows the robot to efficiently plan its path even in complex environments. One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. These p-dopants occupy interstitial positions in the TiO2 lattice, allowing us to investigate their behavior in both oxygen sites adjacent to a Ti site and within the (TiO2) layer spacing. When placed in the space between two titanium atoms, a carbon or nitrogen atom forms a bond with the nearest titanium or oxygen atom, respectively. By contrast, the energy gap remains relatively constant when an interstitial nitrogen atom is placed in the space between two oxygen atoms. Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. We have analyzed the semi-leptonic decays of J/ψ in the context of two types of particle decay: neutrino and dark matter. Specifically, we focused on the process J/ψ decaying into a photon and an invisible lepton pair, which is used to derive upper limits on the products of neutrino or dark matter mass and coupling strength. Furthermore, we show that the walk's behavior around record times is sharply distinguished from its behavior elsewhere. Specifically, in the limit as the record number grows, the local time outside records follows a specific scaling law that depends on the walk's starting point. In contrast, for walks with significant discrepancies, we find the limiting behavior outside records to follow a different scaling law, different from that of walks with minimal deviations. In addition, we establish the walk's local time near its local maximum to have a distribution that converges to a specific non-trivial limit in probability. This finding has implications for various problems related to random walk, including its cover time, distance to the origin, and the time until it first crosses certain barriers. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. A study using a diagnostic tool called the plasma grid analyzer found that it can indeed produce helicon mode, and characterized the resulting plasma as follows: the plasma density varies inversely with the distance from the source, and follows a cosine angular distribution; the electron temperature remains constant at around 3 volts; the ion temperature is higher near the source but equalizes with the electron temperature at around 10 centimeters from the source; the cross-field electron flow is minimal, and the total current matches the sum of the local and cross-field components. A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated program designed to operate across different networks. However, ensuring the accuracy and reliability of these contracts is a significant challenge. To address this issue, the Tezos blockchain utilizes a formal verification approach, involving the use of refinement types to detect potential errors in contracts before deployment. This process involves a two-step procedure where the type of refined values is first defined, and then the type of the program's output is compared to this definition. Based on this comparison, the Helmholtz verifier determines whether the program's output matches its intended refined type, effectively identifying any potential errors in the contract. To facilitate easier detection of errors, the verifier also provides the underlying proof of the error's existence. This verification tool is an example of the capabilities of the Mini-MLC programming language, a simplified version of the MLRISC language that retains the essential features necessary for verification. The Mini-MLC compiler is also discussed, along with an overview of the Refined-ML language and its type system. Additionally, a discussion on the performance of the verifier is presented, along with a sample contract verification scenario. The implementation of the Helmholtz verifier has resulted in the verification of multiple real-world Tezos contracts, with a focus on the Michelson programming language used for Tezos smart contracts. The evaluation of the verifier showed that while it is efficient for small to medium-sized contracts, it can be challenging to verify larger contracts due to the increased complexity. To address this limitation, potential optimizations for the verifier are discussed, along with the possibility of integrating the Mini-MLC compiler with the Michelson compiler to further improve the verification process. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. Moreover, our approach involves updating existing center estimates at a cost of $O(kd)$ operations per update, and determines the initial center set without knowledge of the data distribution. The algorithm's output generates a solution with a final clustering cost within a factor of $O(\sqrt{k})$ of the optimal solution. This achievement builds upon previous work utilizing super-fast coreset construction, and the resulting algorithm exhibits more practical performance in streaming settings. We complement our algorithm with an almost-optimal lower bound showing that any coreset algorithm for $k$-means in data streams requires at least $\Omega(k \log \Delta)$ storage capacity in $d$ dimensions. We further extend our results to $k$-median and facility location problems, obtaining coreset sizes of $O(kd \log \Delta)$. These results provide significant advancements in the field of coreset construction for Euclidean space optimization problems. Finally, we evaluate and verify the performance of our algorithm through extensive experiments on real-world high-dimensional data. Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance in image quality improvement. A key application of this is radiation dose reduction, which has seen the development of several deep learning methods for various medical imaging modalities. In this work, we introduce an unsupervised dose-matching protocol and adapt the cycleGAN framework to upgrade low-dose CT scans to routine-dose scans. Notably, our proposed model builds upon the cycleGAN architecture by incorporating an adaptive instance normalization switch, which allows for both unsupervised training and dose-matching. A numerical study involving CT simulation data demonstrated the effectiveness of our model, achieving a mean absolute error of 10.3 HU, a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 33.6 dB, and a structural similarity index of 0.923 when compared to reference images. Furthermore, our model exhibited competitive performance when compared to other deep learning methods. The implementation of an unsupervised training strategy allowed for a significant reduction in training data, from 1000 to 100 samples per dose level. The proposed model was also evaluated on real-world data, yielding promising results and highlighting potential applications in dose reduction. The code for the model has been made available on GitHub, along with instructions for reproduction. The findings suggest that deep learning techniques have the potential to enhance low-dose CT images, which could contribute to radiation dose reduction. Despite the significant success of pre-trained models in task-oriented dialog understanding, they struggle with conversational datasets that have limited labeled data. To address this challenge, we introduce SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model that utilizes semi-supervised contrastive learning for the understanding of dialog conversations. SPACE-2 is based on the BERT architecture and incorporates a semi-supervised contrastive loss during pre-training. It leverages both labeled and unlabeled dialog data to learn representations that capture the underlying structure of conversational dialogues. During pre-training, SPACE-2 learns to extract task-relevant information from labeled data and incorporates unlabeled dialog data to discover the hidden patterns in conversational dialogues. We evaluate SPACE-2 on the Dialog-State Tracking and MultiTurn Reasoning tasks, achieving notable improvements over the baseline models that rely on supervised pre-training alone. Notably, SPACE-2 achieves a Dialog-State Tracking Task accuracy of 92.3%, outperforming the current state-of-the-art by a 1.5% margin, and a MultiTurn Reasoning Task score of 63.8%, surpassing the current top-performing model by a 3.5% margin. challenging issue in model-based multi-task reinforcement learning is the
catastrophic interference problem, which causes previously learned information to
be lost when learning new tasks. In this study, we demonstrate that using a
modular multi-task reinforcement learning approach, with separate models for
each task and a shared connection network, can substantially reduce the impact of
catastrophic interference. This leads to faster learning and better performance
when learning new tasks. We further show that introducing a shared representation
can help to some extent, but this improvement is mostly attributed to the use
of a shared connection network in this setup. We validate our findings with a
series of simulated robotic learning scenarios, as well as real-world data
collected from a 4D end-to-end driving dataset. The results show that modular
learning can result in a 50% reduction in the number of experiences required

implications for solving complex multi-task reinforcement learning problems in
real-world applications. This research is the first to explore the benefits of a

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint the exact location of sounds within an image frame. Unlike previous approaches that rely on supplementary information or specific categories of sounds, we aim to tackle this challenge for all sounds. To achieve this, we've developed a method to automatically train a sound-anchoring model using a single dataset containing paired images and sounds. To evaluate our method's effectiveness, we conducted two experiments: one focused on identifying the bounding box and another on pinpointing the exact pixel location within that box. Our results indicate that our approach outperforms existing models and redresses the disparity between sound- and object-localization tasks. Furthermore, our method demonstrates robustness in handling a diverse range of sounds and challenging visual scenes. To facilitate further research, we're introducing a new dataset called VisualSound-500, comprising 500 pairs of sounds and images. This dataset is available for download on our project website. Alongside this, we've conducted an in-depth analysis of sound-features and discovered that certain features contribute significantly to the difficulty of this task. To overcome this, we propose a novel approach that involves feature-reweighting, resulting in substantial improvements in accuracy. Lastly, our findings suggest that current models fall short in localizing sounds with complex semantic meanings. To address this, we propose a new protocol for evaluating the performance of sound-anchoring models and provide a comparative analysis of existing methods against our proposed method. This research aims to address the long-standing issue of sound-anchoring in computer vision and paves the way for further advancements in this area. This method can identify the specific features altered during image processing and estimate the impact on disease predictions.
